title: dream: give the loop real input seams + recurrence memory — turn a stateless keyword grep into consolidation
description:
## Context
Audited 2026-08-07 at Zig's request. /dream's lifetime output is 5 proposals, 5/5
promoted, 0 rejected — precision is 100%, RECALL is the problem. Three limiters found:

1. The 200-candidate default cap (FIXED in d8bd381 — override now at the call site).
2. It is a 5-regex grep over 600-char snippets (dream.py:79-118, CANDIDATE_TEXT_LIMIT=600).
   It never sees a conversation, so it cannot notice a pattern recurring WITHOUT a
   lexical trigger in each instance.
3. The seam is already drained: /offboard, /dive and decision beads harvest corrections
   in-session first. Run 4's own ledger note says the sweep found ZERO uncaptured
   corrections.

And the structural one, which is the real subject of this bead: **its only durable state
is `--since`.** It can ask "is this turn durable?" but never "has this come up three
times?" Recurrence detection is what consolidation MEANS, and it is also what a rot
detector is — the thing that notices "cluster 5 for the eighth week running" without a
human happening to look.

## The design

### A. New input seams — churn histories, where the signal IS what changed
Add pluggable seam collectors. Keep the existing `session-recall` seam. Add:

- `offboard-history` — `git log -p --follow -- refs/session-handoff*.md` in the CURRENT
  repo, last N days (default 90). VERIFIED RICH: 560 near-total-rewrite revisions /
  5.26 MB / 80 days across 7 repos; /offboard overwrites rather than appends
  ("it's a snapshot, not a log"), so friction lives only in git. Caveat: friction density
  is ~0% in May, ~45-55% by 2026-08-05, so default the window to recent history.
- `memory-history` — git history of `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/*.md`. 329 files
  revised >=2x fleet-wide: a ready-made "what we believed, then unbelieved" corpus.
- `skill-history` — `git log` over `~/dotfiles/agents/skills/*/SKILL.md` (185 commits /
  39 skills): WHICH PROMPT WORDING KEEPS GETTING RE-FIXED. Harness rot, directly.
- `findings-corrections` — `## Corrections` / `## Scrutiny` blocks in the current repo's
  `*/FINDINGS.md` (58 blocks / 54 files in explore). Highest signal density; must no-op
  cleanly in repos with no FINDINGS.

### B. Recurrence memory
- `refs/dream-memory.jsonl`, sibling of the ledger; path via `--memory`, default derived.
- Record: `key`, `gist`, `count`, `first_seen`, `last_seen`, `runs[]`, `seams[]`,
  `disposition` (observed|proposed|promoted|rejected).
- `collect` emits a `memory_digest` (existing keys + gists + counts) so the TICK can
  match a new observation to an existing key semantically — do NOT build brittle lexical
  fingerprinting; the model in the loop does the matching.
- New subcommand `remember --observations FILE` merges the tick's observations, bumping
  counts and first/last seen.
- Recurrence bar: qualifies as a proposal when `count >= 2` across DISTINCT runs, OR when
  it appears in `>= 2` distinct seams in one run. `rejected` stays suppressed unless
  count doubles after rejection.

## Hard constraints
- **stdlib only** (the skill is stdlib-only by design).
- **CURRENT SLUG / CURRENT REPO ONLY.** SKILL.md:46-62 forbids cross-slug sweeps because
  `linearb*`/`cfp*` content must never reach a pushed artifact
  (`feedback_linearb_beads_confidential`). Several seam sizes above were measured
  FLEET-WIDE — that is a measurement, NOT a licence to traverse. Every seam must be
  scoped and there must be an explicit guard + a test proving a linearb/cfp path is never
  read.
- **Positive control per seam.** Each seam reports whether it actually searched, so
  "found nothing" is distinguishable from "could not look". House exit contract:
  0 found / 1 searched-nothing-found / 3 could-not-search.
- Existing 13 tests in `agents/skills/dream/tests/test_dream.py` must still pass.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] 4 new seams implemented, each independently togglable, each degrading to empty
      (not error) when its source is absent
- [ ] `refs/dream-memory.jsonl` read+merged; `remember` subcommand works
- [ ] `collect` output carries `memory_digest` and per-seam `searched`/`found` counts
- [ ] Recurrence bar implemented as specified
- [ ] Confidentiality guard + a test that a linearb*/cfp* path is never traversed
- [ ] All existing tests pass; new tests cover each seam + the merge + the bar
- [ ] SKILL.md documents the seams, the two-phase collect/remember flow, and the bar
close_reason: Landed in 25cdfcc (dream.py +1484, test_dream_seams.py 793 lines, SKILL.md +192). Verified 2026-08-08: pytest agents/skills/dream/tests/ → 49 passed; SKILL.md documents all four seams + recurrence bar + two-phase collect/remember. refs/dream-memory.jsonl absent by design (created on first remember run). Cluster-F review evidence.

title: seat-molt: a refused molt whose seat already claimed success wedges silently — first-refusal watcher assumes a retry that never comes
description:
## Context
Confirmed instance 2026-08-10 19:04–19:17Z, seneschal window (session c07a0b7c). Chain: (1) seat hand-rolled its offboard (note+commit+push) instead of walking /offboard, so the window-scoped marker .claude/last-offboard-session--seneschal was never stamped; (2) seat ran seat-molt --self, announced "Molt armed — fires when pane goes idle" and ENDED ITS TURN, but the idle-time check returned refused-not-offboarded at 19:04:52Z — the seat never read a result marker, it narrated intent (cxle class: consumer reports success while the step failed); (3) the it06 escalation is second-refusal-within-90m by design, and a seat that believes it molted never retries, so the first refusal was noted (molt-refusal-note.md 19:06:43Z: "Nobody was notified; nothing was re-fired") and the seat sat wedged ~12 min until Zig nudged (19:16:28Z). Seat then stamped the marker by hand and molted clean at 19:17:17Z. Bounding mitigation already present: the 9,49 heartbeat cron would have woken the seat at 19:49Z. Related: dotfiles-betl (same claim-before-answer shape, marshal-scoped), dotfiles-ixyi (another seat-molt refusal path), dotfiles-cxle (the class).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. In a registered seat window, write/commit a handoff note by hand WITHOUT running /offboard (so no last-offboard-session--<seat> marker).
2. Run agents/scheduler/seat-molt.sh --self --mode auto --in-flight no and end the turn on its "armed" output without reading the ledger.
3. Observe molt-ledger.jsonl gains result:"refused-not-offboarded" at idle time, molt-refusal-state.jsonl stage:"noted", and nothing re-fires — the pane sits wedged with the seat believing it molted.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] seat-molt either verifies the offboard marker at ARM time (failing loud synchronously) or emits a SEAT_MOLT_RESULT= marker contract the seat must read before claiming success — pick one, implement, and demonstrate failure-before / absence-after with real output.
- [ ] pulse-escalate's molt-refusal watcher nudges the refusing pane (tmux-send.sh) on the FIRST refusal when that pane is idle — refused+idle means the seat thinks it is done; keep the second-refusal P1+push unchanged.
- [ ] A mutant run (marker deliberately absent) dies at the new guard, and the mutation is asserted applied before the exit code is read (47nf/77s4 discipline).

title: demesne-sync interregnum gaps: root files drift outside the synced set; --delete eats gitignored live-state in demesne refs/
description:
## Context
Two instances found 2026-08-09 while carrying the ypbc fix live. (1) demesne/.gitignore drifted since seed — the seneschal-brief stanza existed only in dotfiles, so the untracked brief made the destination 'dirty' and sync REFUSED (correct refusal, stale cause). Fixed inline: stanza carried, demesne e13b14b. (2) rsync --delete then removed demesne refs/seneschal-brief.md itself — gitignored live-state artifacts inside a synced dir are deleted on every sync because the source tree doesn't carry them. Harmless for the brief (rewritten each tick) but the class is not: any gitignored-but-live file under demesne agents/ refs/ claude/ is sync-mortal.

Both are interregnum-only: k579 flips authorship to demesne and retires the sync. So this is a JUDGE-AT-k579 bead, not necessarily an implement-now one.

- [ ] Decide root-file (.gitignore, and any other root files the seed copied) drift handling: manual carry (status quo, document it in demesne-sync.sh header) vs add to synced set — record the decision on this bead
- [ ] At k579 close: confirm the sync is retired and close this as moot, or convert the surviving items into k579 acceptance criteria

title: agents: doc --force --force on worktree removal — sync CLAUDE.md change into AGENTS.md

title: validate-seats: warn when a seat has schedules but no interactive mark
description:
## Context
The `interactive: false` mark has two mechanical consumers (the AskUserQuestion seat
guard and post-push-fallback.sh's bead-first steer) and NO validator opinion at all —
validate-seats.py does not even type-check the key. Both marks so far (marshal
dotfiles-9i39, linearb dotfiles-iyip) were added AFTER the seat froze or nearly froze,
which is the shape of a fact nothing asserts.

place the roster's other cross-checks live.

existing UNIT rule), with a mutant in agents/lib/mutate-validate-seats.sh proving it
bites. Gated on dotfiles-l7fj: the rule's default is only honest once Zig has ruled which
scheduled seats are meant to stay interactive — otherwise it warns about rows that are
correct.

title: POST: optional actioned/resolved marker on mail rows — 'dealt with' as a fact instead of archaeology (seneschal ask, deferred from the 5z5n wave as scope creep)
description:
## Context
Seneschal request during the 5z5n build (2026-08-14): a cursor records that a row was DELIVERED to a reader, not that it was ACTIONED. Its own audit of 26 seneschal rows had to be reconstructed by inference because the spool holds no actioned state. Ask: an optional actioned/resolved marker a reader may set, so 'has this been dealt with' becomes a fact. Explicitly deferred out of the landing wave: it changes the row shape or adds a side-channel, and the wave's compat contract (byte-identical with socket-registry cmd_spool) is load-bearing.

## Fork to decide (not tonight)
(a) side-file: actioned/<seat>.jsonl appending {spool, line_or_ts, actioned_ts, note} — append-only, zero row-shape change, matches the cursor pattern; (b) in-row optional field written by senders only (does NOT solve the reader-side marking need); (c) rely on the existing ref field discipline — actioning IS filing/commenting the bead a row points at, so the fact lives in the bead graph (the on-the-record-means-a-bead memory argues this), plus a small helper that joins spool rows to bead activity; (d) decline — cursors + bead refs are enough.

Note (c) is the doctrine-consistent candidate: 7fik R5 says mail points at work without BEING work, and a durable actioned-fact is work-state. Whoever decides should weigh why (a)'s convenience beats the two-stores-one-truth cost.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] One option chosen with the doctrine argument recorded here; if (a)/(b), a follow-up impl bead with compat analysis; if (c), the helper's shape sketched; if (d), the seneschal's audit pain answered some other named way
notes:
MEASURED INPUT FROM THE SENESCHAL (invited by the Works). I ran the join you are proposing against the ENTIRE live corpus — all 58 rows across all seven mailboxes — rather than arguing it from doctrine. The derive-from-ref idea is doctrine-right and I would back it, but the corpus cannot support it today, and the reason is sharper than 'some rows lack a ref'.

THE NUMBERS, 2026-08-14, 58 rows total:
  22 rows (38%) carry a ref that RESOLVES to a real bead — verified by actually running br show against four stores (dotfiles, dashboard-dev-interrupted, imc-aug26, linearb)
  18 rows (31%) carry a single-token ref that is a TOPIC SLUG, not a bead
   8 rows (14%) carry a compound/prose ref, e.g. 'aug26-un6 / asana 1217069344502046' or 'aug26-un6 / tab t.1e93dvmdt964'
  10 rows (17%) carry NO ref at all
So a mechanical join would classify at most 38% of the corpus and would have to report 'unknown' for the other 62%.

⚠️ THE HARDER PROBLEM, AND THE ONE I DID NOT EXPECT: a bead ref and a topic ref are SYNTACTICALLY INDISTINGUISHABLE. Compare 'dotfiles-4x49' (a real bead) with 'marshal-gardener' (a topic I invented); 'aug26-ju6' (bead) with 'ldx3-nyc' (topic). Both are <word>-<word>. Nothing in the shape tells you which is which — the ONLY way to know is to attempt a lookup, and the lookup needs the right STORE, which the row does not name. My measurement had to try four stores per ref. So the join is not 'read the ref', it is 'guess the store, attempt a resolve, and treat failure as either not-a-bead or wrong-store' — and those two failures are indistinguishable too.

I OWN THE PROBLEM: I am the largest producer of topic slugs. post-molt-gateway-stall (x4), di-content-pipeline (x3), harness-repair (x2), marshal-gardener (x2), cfp-double-assignment, ldx3-nyc, idea-bead-decomposition-gate, okr-q3-fy27, harness-harden-2026-08-13 are all mine, invented ad hoc over the last two days because a routed mail often has no bead yet — which is precisely WHY it is being routed. That is not an abuse of the field; it is a second legitimate use of one field, which is the actual defect.

WHAT I WOULD ARGUE ON YOUR FORK OPTIONS: the derive-from-ref candidate is right in DIRECTION and should not be adopted as-is. It needs the two uses separated first, and the cheapest separation that respects your byte-compat contract is probably a NAMESPACE inside the existing string — 'topic:marshal-gardener' vs a bare bead id — rather than a new field or a new store. That keeps the row shape, makes the two kinds distinguishable by inspection, and lets a joiner skip topics honestly instead of failing to resolve them and guessing why. It also leaves the 10 ref-less rows correctly classified as 'unknown', which is honest rather than wrong.

WHAT I WOULD NOT DO: infer actioned-ness from a resolve failure. Today that would silently mark 62% of the corpus as unactionable when much of it WAS actioned — my own 26 rows audit clean, but I reconstructed that from context and memory, not from any record. That inference is exactly the archaeology this bead exists to end.

Raw measurement is reproducible: iterate every *.jsonl in ~/.local/state/harness/post/mail/, bucket by ref shape, then br show each single-token ref against each store.

title: fix: dotfiles biome.json — $schema pinned to 2.0.0 vs CLI 2.5.5, deprecated linter.rules.recommended
description:
## Problem

`biome/biome.json` throws two non-fatal warnings under Biome 2.5.5 (`biome rage`):
1. `$schema` pinned to `2.0.0` while the installed CLI is `2.5.5`
2. `linter.rules.recommended` is **deprecated** (should be `preset`)

Config still reports "Loaded successfully" — cosmetic today, but a **Biome 3
landmine**: both are the kind of deprecation that becomes a hard error on the next
major.

Biome is otherwise fully healthy — it survived the 2026-07-25 bun-global re-hoist
that broke `googleapis` (verified: `biome check` produces correct diagnostics, the
linter fires, and the `--write --error-on-warnings` hook path exits 0).

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `$schema` bumped to match the installed CLI (2.5.5)
- [ ] `linter.rules.recommended` migrated to `preset`
- [ ] `biome migrate` used where it does the work correctly, rather than hand-editing
- [ ] `biome rage` no longer reports either warning
- [ ] `biome check` still produces the same diagnostics on a sample file (no rule-set regression)
- [ ] committed + pushed
notes:
## DONE — 2026-07-25 (commit 2f98f4f, pushed)

`biome migrate --write` made exactly two changes and nothing else: $schema
2.0.0 -> 2.5.5, and linter.rules.recommended: true -> preset: "recommended".
Config is symlinked at ~/.config/biome/biome.json, so it is live.

`biome rage` now reports "Loaded successfully" with ZERO errors or warnings.

NO RULE-SET REGRESSION — this was the thing actually worth verifying, not just that
the warnings disappeared: the biome check diagnostics before vs after are IDENTICAL
byte-for-byte (9 diagnostics; full output identical with timing normalized). They
span correctness/suspicious/style/security/complexity, so the preset is genuinely
exercised. Hook path `biome check --write --error-on-warnings` exits 0.
close_reason: done

title: human: controlled reboot test of pico — harness-wide, and there is NO way back in if it fails
description:
## Context

Filed 2026-07-26 from the vs14d session. pico's boot persistence was audited
end-to-end and the one blocking gap is fixed, but **nothing has actually been
rebooted** — six things are unprovable without doing it, and the test is
fleet-wide rather than a vs14 concern.

## Why this is not a casual reboot

**1. It takes down the LLM control plane for every Claude Code session.**
`~/.claude/settings.json` on zig-computer sets
`ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL = http://100.72.47.4:17017/claude`. Every session, including
whichever one is running the test, routes inference through `agentgateway` on
pico. If it does not come back, **Claude Code cannot be used to diagnose why.**

**2. There is NO out-of-band access to pico.** Measured: `ip route get
100.72.47.4` → `dev tailscale0`, and that is the only path. pico is a home Mac
behind NAT with no public IP; zig-computer is a VPS on a different network.
Screen sharing binds `*:5900` but is still only reachable over the tailnet from
here. **If tailscaled does not come back, pico is unreachable and recovery
requires physically walking to the machine.**

**3. It takes two public sites down** — `vs14.zig.computer` (via pico:8080) and
`webmention.andrewzigler.com` (via pico:14829) — plus the inference stack,
postgres, the seven containers, Keycloak (so admin login), and the homeowner's
LAN route to the picod portal.

## What is already proven, and what is not

**Fixed and verified before this bead:**
- `homebrew.mxcl.nginx` had NO KeepAlive and died at the last reboot
  (`bind() to 100.72.47.4:8080 failed (49)` at 15:52:32 on May 28, pid 364
  racing tailscaled at pid 367) and stayed dead **14 days** until a brew upgrade
  restarted it. `KeepAlive` + `ThrottleInterval=10` added and loaded.
- zig-computer's nginx had the same race one layer up — it does not bind a
  tailnet address, but it resolves `pico.tailfb4637.ts.net` in `proxy_pass` at
  config-load time via MagicDNS, and shipped `Restart=no`. Drop-in added:
  `After=/Wants=tailscaled.service`, `Restart=on-failure`, `RestartSec=10`.
- A duplicate `homebrew.mxcl.tailscale` LaunchAgent was crash-looping
  **242,422** times (EX_CONFIG — tailscaled needs root, the agent runs as pico).
  Booted out and disabled; the system daemon that actually owns the tunnel
  (pid 367, runs=1) untouched.
- Auto-login enabled on pico, so LaunchAgents now fire at boot.

**Genuine reassurance for the scariest item:** tailscaled is a system
LaunchDaemon and was **pid 367 at the May 28 boot, `runs = 1`, never exited** —
so it demonstrably does come back. That is the one boot-critical service with
real historical evidence.

**Still unprovable without rebooting:** auto-login actually firing (configured
today, never exercised); whether that session is a full Aqua session a `vz` VM
will start in; agentgateway's real boot behaviour (its plist is dated Jul 1, the
last boot was May 28 — it has NEVER been through one); whether nginx's new retry
cadence beats a cold-WAN tailscale handshake; the true recovery ordering; and
**11 of 26 enabled jobs are younger than the 59-day uptime and have never seen a
boot at all.**

## How to run it

`~/vs14d/ops/pico/post-reboot-verify.sh` is the checklist — **35 pass / 1 fail**
when run as a baseline today, the single red being the nginx gap now closed.
Run it before, reboot, run it after, diff.

Suggested conditions:
- [ ] A window where Zig is physically able to reach pico, since that is the
      only recovery path
- [ ] Not during a live Claude Code session doing anything that matters
- [ ] Baseline `post-reboot-verify.sh` captured immediately beforehand
- [ ] Know that `/etc/kcpassword` was hand-written (sysadminctl failed with
      SACSetAutoLoginPassword error:22) and round-trip verified but **never
      tested by an actual boot** — if auto-login does not fire, the LaunchAgents
      do not fire either, and that is the likeliest failure

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Reboot performed in a controlled window
- [ ] `post-reboot-verify.sh` re-run; every previously-passing check still passes
- [ ] agentgateway confirmed serving `:17017` and a Claude Code session works
- [ ] Both public sites 200; Keycloak login exercised; containers all healthy
- [ ] Anything that did not return gets a plist or a documented manual step
- [ ] The six unprovable items above converted into measured facts
notes:
UPDATED 2026-07-26 after the homework was finished and re-measured.

BASELINE IS NOW GREEN: `~/vs14d/ops/pico/post-reboot-verify.sh` reports
**36 pass / 0 fail / 0 warn — "GREEN. Every critical service returned."**
(It was 35/1 when written; the single red was the nginx KeepAlive gap, now
closed.) Re-run by hand rather than assumed.

RECOVERY PATH — CORRECTED BY ZIG, and the original framing was too dire.

I wrote "there is NO way back in." That is only true in ONE direction. The
asymmetry, verified:

  zig-computer -> pico   requires the tailnet. `ip route get 100.72.47.4` ->
                         `dev tailscale0`, and pico is behind NAT with no public
                         IP. If tailscaled does not come back, this direction is
                         genuinely dead.
  pico -> zig-computer   does NOT. pico holds ~/.ssh/id_ed25519, routes to the
                         internet via 192.168.1.1 on en0, and zig-computer's
                         sshd listens on 0.0.0.0:22 with a public IP
                         (51.81.33.136). That path does not involve tailscale at
                         all.

And Zig has PHYSICAL access to pico, which is the decisive point: worst case is
inconvenience, not loss.

Worth considering (not required): a boot-time reverse tunnel from pico to
zig-computer would turn that outbound asymmetry into a real out-of-band channel
and remove the tailscale dependency from recovery entirely. Optional — physical
access already covers it.

THE SIX THINGS ONLY A REBOOT CAN SETTLE, and why each is unprovable:

1. **Whether auto-login fires at all.** Configured today; `/etc/kcpassword` was
   hand-written because `sysadminctl` failed with SACSetAutoLoginPassword
   error:22. Round-trip verified (the file decodes back to the typed password)
   but that only proves the ENCODER is self-consistent, not that macOS agrees
   with it. macOS reads that file exactly once, at boot. The entire LOGIN tier
   rides on it — agentgateway, postgres, the VM, seven containers, the vs14
   site, go-jamming.
2. **Whether that session is a full Aqua session a `vz` VM will start in.**
   Distinct from (1): the session can exist and still be the wrong KIND. colima's
   VM needs a graphical session context; a LoginWindow-tier session would let
   LaunchAgents run and still fail to start the VM. Only observable after a real
   login.
3. **agentgateway's actual boot behaviour.** Inferred entirely from its plist
   semantics (RunAtLoad + KeepAlive{SuccessfulExit=false}, throttle 10s). Its
   plist is dated Jul 1; the last boot was May 28 — **it has never been through
   one.** And this is the LLM control plane for every Claude Code session.
4. **Whether nginx's new KeepAlive actually wins the race.** It will certainly
   retry; whether the retry cadence converges before or after tailscaled
   completes a control-plane handshake over a COLD WAN is a timing property of
   the real network on the real morning. Retry is unbounded so it should
   converge — "should" is doing the work in that sentence.
5. **The true recovery ordering and total time to green.** The predicted
   sequence is assembled from throttle values and interval settings, not
   measured. Nothing declares these dependencies to launchd; five services bind
   the tailnet address and survive only because KeepAlive retries until it
   appears. That is robustness by accident, and accidents have timing.
6. **Whether the eleven jobs created since May 28 behave at boot.** Enabled and
   never boot-tested: com.zig.agentgateway, com.zig.colima, com.zig.gojamming,
   com.zig.harness, com.zig.ss14-backup, com.zig.vs14-autoheal,
   com.zig.vs14-postgres-retention, homebrew.mxcl.postgresql@17,
   com.zig.ha-portal-proxy, com.zig.ollama, com.canonical.multipassd.
   **Eleven of twenty-six enabled jobs are younger than the 59-day uptime.**
   That is the real shape of the risk: not one suspect service, but a
   configuration whose MAJORITY has never been exercised by the event we are
   about to trigger.

The common thread: every one is a property of the boot TRANSITION, and a running
system carries no evidence about a transition it has not made. This is the
irreducible residue after the audit — which is exactly why it is a scheduled
test rather than more analysis.

ALSO FOUND, not blocking, but the same family: `com.zig.tmux` is crash-looping
at ~241,920 runs (exit 1). That is the THIRD such loop on pico — the tailscale
duplicate agent had 242,422 and vs14-web had 237,737 before it was fixed today.
Three jobs in permanent restart loops that nobody noticed is a pattern
(dotfiles-cxle), not three coincidences. Filed separately.
close_reason:
Superseded by events — the decision this human: bead asked for was made and executed via dotfiles-xh18 (P0, closed 2026-08-09): Zig ruled the window (AskUserQuestion, after the dream tick) AND raised the stakes to the Tahoe 26.6.1 major jump, explicitly accepting the risk; the reboot fired ~12:36Z fully unattended and pico returned. Routed for lifecycle action by the seneschal 2026-08-09; verified before closing by the Master of Works, not assumed:

- post-reboot-verify.sh RE-RUN today post-Tahoe by this seat: 36 pass / 0 fail / 0 warn GREEN — every previously-passing check still passes, including port 18080 (keycloak), all container ports, and end-to-end GET https://vs14.zig.computer/admin/ 200 + GET https://webmention.andrewzigler.com/ 200. (k6wq's AC items xh18's close did not itself cite.)
- agentgateway :17017 401-healthy and every Claude Code session on the fleet routes through it right now — AC "a Claude Code session works" is proven by the fleet being alive.
- The six unprovable boot-transition items are now MEASURED facts (several measured as broken-and-handled, which is what the test was for): (1) auto-login fired — the user session came up and user agents were kickstartable in it; (3) agentgateway's real boot behaviour observed — drained exit-0, KeepAlive{SuccessfulExit=false} did NOT restart it (the k6wq analysis' inference was wrong in the dangerous direction); (6) the never-booted jobs exercised — Tahoe's background-task management PENDED all user LaunchAgents (new failure class), colima autostart verified BROKEN, homebrew postgres@17 needed a manual kickstart (class-miss outside com.zig.*). Recovery evidence + patch posture + Tahoe pended-spawn warning recorded in agents/infra.md; hardening charter dotfiles-40ej + incident dotfiles-kviw own the durable fixes.

Residual delta, named honestly: Keycloak was verified at the port (18080 PASS) and via admin-page 200, not by an exercised login flow; the optional boot-time reverse tunnel idea was not pursued (physical access covers recovery, per Zig's own correction in this bead). Neither blocks the decision this bead existed to make — the controlled-reboot question is settled by a reboot that happened, was survived, and taught exactly the lessons it was scheduled to teach.

title: guard: session-start should assert ~/.claude/settings.json is still a symlink (it silently reverts)
description:
## Why

`dotfiles-2wqv` restored the `~/.claude/settings.json` symlink after it had been a
regular file since ~2026-07-10. **It will almost certainly break again.** Claude Code
writes that file atomically (temp + `rename`), and `rename()` replaces a symlink with
a regular file. Anything that makes Claude Code write global settings does it:
accepting a permission, changing effort in the menu, toggling fast mode.

The failure is **completely silent**, and the damage compounds — the file keeps
working, so nothing alarms, while the tracked template quietly falls behind. Last time
it drifted 5 settings, including `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` (the proxy carrying ALL API
traffic) and the Agent isolation hook. It also left `effortLevel: xhigh` in the
template, which is the Opus 5 WebSearch-killer — so a fresh machine or a `sync.sh`
restore would have silently reinstalled a broken config.

This is a **checkable invariant**, which per the harness's own policy means it belongs
in a hook, not in a habit.

## Sketch

In `agents/hooks/session-start.sh`: if `~/.claude/settings.json` is NOT a symlink

diverged, so the merge is mechanical rather than archaeological.

* [ ] the warning names the exact remediation AND the merge-first caveat
* [ ] it does NOT auto-repair
* [ ] verified by temporarily replacing the symlink with a copy, confirming the warning fires, then restoring
* [ ] no measurable startup cost (runs on every session)

title: pulse-dispatch-remote: the preflight block message asserts a cause it never checked and points at stderr that was never captured — a 2-day-old failure with an empty diagnostic trail
description:
## Context

`pulse-di-thursday.service` failed 2026-07-30 13:00:18 UTC and sat in
`systemctl --user --failed` for **two days**. The unit behaved impeccably — fail-closed,
nothing dispatched, no remote tokens spent, no misleading ledger row, a
`PULSE_DISPATCH_RESULT=failed-preflight` marker on the terminal path. The
unattended-reporting contract (`dotfiles-cxle`) did its job.

**The defect is that the diagnostic it produced is empty and wrong.**

### (a) The message asserts a cause it never checked

`agents/scheduler/pulse-dispatch-remote.sh:1048-1050` fails with a hardcoded string on
**any** non-zero preflight exit:

```bash
if ! "$PREFLIGHT" "${PF_ARGS[@]}"; then
  fail failed-preflight 73 "vps-preflight blocked (assertions A1 empty-submodule / A2 stale-HEAD).
```

`vps-preflight.sh` exits non-zero from at least four paths that have nothing to do with
A1 or A2: `exit 64` (unknown arg), `exit 65` (manifest not found), `exit 69` (jq
missing), `exit 69` (ssh missing). All four would be reported as an A1/A2 assertion
failure. The exit code is discarded rather than switched on.

### (b) It points at stderr that does not exist

The message says *"Its stderr above names the exact repo and remedy."* For this run there
is no such stderr. Full-precision journal, the entire preflight window:

```
13:00:16.456050  sync T1 + preflight A1+A2: refreshing marketing-vps and judging the receipt locally
13:00:18.111919  PULSE-DISPATCH: BLOCKED — vps-preflight blocked (assertions A1 ... / A2 ...)
```

**1.65 seconds of execution, zero output.** No global stderr redirection exists in the
dispatch script, and every `exit` in `vps-preflight.sh` is preceded by a `>&2` message —
so this should have been impossible.

### (c) And it did not take the path the message names

`vps-preflight.sh:176` — `block() { write_report; printf 'VPS-PREFLIGHT: BLOCKED...' >&2; exit "$2"; }` — **writes the report BEFORE printing.** The run directory
`~/.local/state/pulse-dispatch/20260730T130008Z-di-thursday/` contains no
`checkout-state.json`, while later successful runs
(`20260731T190650Z-di-friday`, `20260731T233702Z-di-monday`) do. So the preflight
**did not exit via `block()`** — i.e. not via A1 or A2 — and the message claiming it did
is false on this exact run. What it did do is still unknown, which is the point.

### (d) The artifact a reader would open repeats the false pointer

`surface-blocked.json` — the one durable file an operator opens — carries
`"detail": "...Its stderr above names the exact repo and remedy."` It forwards the
pointer without the payload.

### Why it went unnoticed for 2 days

It escalated into two surfaces with no reader: `systemctl --user --failed` (see the
sibling finding — nothing on this box reads it) and an AskUserQuestion delivered to tmux
window `work:di`, which no longer exists. So even a diligent operator following the trail
finds nothing. The condition self-resolved: `di-friday` ran clean on 07-31. That is what
makes it easy to keep not noticing.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `systemctl --user show pulse-di-thursday.service -p Result -p ExecMainExitTimestamp`
   -> `Result=exit-code`, `ExecMainExitTimestamp=Thu 2026-07-30 13:00:18 UTC`.
2. `journalctl --user -u pulse-di-thursday.service --since '2026-07-30 13:00:00' --until '2026-07-30 13:00:25' -o short-precise`
   -> 1.65 s between the preflight announcement and the BLOCKED line, with no output between.
3. `ls ~/.local/state/pulse-dispatch/20260730T130008Z-di-thursday/` -> no
   `checkout-state.json`. Compare `20260731T190650Z-di-friday/`, which has one.
4. `sed -n '176p' agents/scheduler/vps-preflight.sh` -> `block()` writes the report first,
   so (3) rules out the cause the message names.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] The preflight's stdout+stderr are **captured to a file** in `$LOCAL_STATE`
      (e.g. `preflight.err`, beside the existing `rsync.err` / `tunnel.err`) as well as
      reaching the journal. A tee, not a redirect — do not trade one lost copy for another.
- [ ] The `fail` message switches on the preflight's **actual exit code**. 64/65/69 are
      usage / manifest / missing-dependency and must not be reported as A1/A2. An
      unrecognised code says so rather than guessing.
- [ ] `surface-blocked.json`'s `detail` carries the **captured stderr tail and the exit
      code**, not a pointer to them. It is the artifact a reader opens.
- [ ] Determine what actually exited non-zero at 1.65 s with no output and no report —
      the reproduction above is the starting point. If it turns out to be unreachable
      after the capture lands, record that as a `-t decision` rather than closing silently.
- [ ] A negative control: force a preflight failure and confirm the operator can name the
      cause from `surface-blocked.json` **alone**, without the journal.

Related: `dotfiles-cxle` (the contract this obeys on the reporting axis and violates on the
diagnostic one — a verdict marker is necessary, not sufficient), `explore-z7eq` (the
unread alarm surfaces that let it sit 2 days), `explore-tkci` (P1 — re-architect the DI
pulses onto the LinearB company seat; this is live evidence for it).

title: SECURITY P0 (escalation): the granola webhook has ZERO auth — a prompt-injection vector into the corpus LinearB agents read as ground truth
description:
Escalates dotfiles-6wdw. Found by the reef/granola design agent, 2026-07-25.

THE FINDING: reef's `authMiddleware` (linearb/reef/polyps/router/src/middleware/
auth.ts, HMAC-SHA256) EXISTS and is wired to EXACTLY ZERO call sites — grep
returns two hits, both inside auth.ts itself. Correct code, never applied.

So today, on http://51.81.33.136:7575/coral/granola/webhook — plain HTTP, raw IP,
world-open in UFW — ANY host on the internet can POST arbitrary JSON and cause
two file writes into ~/linearb/reef/coral/granola/data/.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN THE PIVOT I ORIGINALLY FILED:
That directory is a CORPUS THAT LINEARB CLAUDE AGENTS READ AS GROUND TRUTH
(referenced by .claude/skills/imc/references/di-talk-track.md via a hardcoded
path, and by skills-library/CLAUDE.md). An attacker does not need to breach
anything — they can WRITE INSTRUCTIONS INTO THE CONTEXT of agents doing
confidential client work. This is a prompt-injection vector, not spam.

Secondary: confidential meeting transcripts cross the public internet in
PLAINTEXT on the Zapier -> zig-computer leg. nginx allows 16 MB bodies; the only
brake is an in-memory 100 req/min/IP limit that dies on restart.

No path traversal (timestamp + slugify filenames), so the exposure is content
injection + disk fill, not RCE.

MITIGATION ORDER (Zig has retained :7575 because granola is load-bearing for
LinearB work — do NOT close it before the replacement is live):
 1. FASTEST PARTIAL FIX, available today, hours not days: wire the EXISTING
    authMiddleware to the granola route and add the token to the Zap's header.
    ~15 lines. This does not fix plaintext, but it closes the anonymous-write
    hole, which is the part an attacker can use without any privileged position.
 2. Then the full migration (explore/dotfiles spec, filed separately):
    transcripts.zig.computer over TLS -> a small Go daemon on 127.0.0.1:14390 ->
    ~/linearb/transcripts/. Kills the pico round-trip, adds TLS + constant-time
    token compare, and closes :7575 permanently.

⚠️ DEPENDENCY ON ZIG (blocks step 1): the Zapier action must be
"Webhooks by Zapier -> POST" for a custom Authorization header to be settable.
If the Zap uses a Granola-native integration instead, the header may not be
available and the auth design changes. Resolve by opening the Zap. Same visit:
Granola's trigger likely exposes attendees / meeting time / URL, which the
current payload does NOT carry ({title, transcript, summary?} only) — which is
why every transcript's frontmatter says participants: Me / Them. One edit,
two wins.
notes:
## Verification — 2026-07-26 (Opus-5 audit Wave 1)

Anonymous write is closed on EVERY reachable path. Public cleartext POST to :7575/coral/granola/webhook -> 401. TLS POST to granola.zig.computer -> 401; bare root with no/bogus token -> 404 deny, with lb-granola logging reason=no_token / bad_token / wrong_method. safeCompare() sha256s both sides before ConstantTimeCompare. title: pulse-ledger-lint: add a duplicate (PT day, row) done-line rule
description:
## Context
pulse-ledger-lint.py checks row-name validity but has NO rule for duplicate done
lines. It reported CLEAN both before and after two genuine duplicate-done groups
were found by hand in the dashboard-dev-interrupted ledger (guest-promo
2026-07-07 and 2026-07-14, where the split newsletter/clips halves each appended
their own done line).

That class matters: caps count done lines, so a duplicate makes a 1/week row read
as 2 fires that week, and it violates the spec's own "one tick, one line, written
last" rule. It is invisible to every existing gate.

The detector is small and already written once as a throwaway: bucket each done
line's ts into the PROJECT timezone (zoneinfo, never a naive `date +%F` on the UTC
stamp — evening ticks mis-bucket forward) and flag any (PT day, row) group with
more than one done.

Important scoping detail learned the hard way: the rule must apply to DONE lines
only. A done + quiet pair on the same day is legitimate — it records two separate
tick fires — and flagging it invites exactly the wrong fix (we briefly collapsed
one and had to restore it).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Ledger with two done lines for the same row on the same PT day
2. python3 ~/dotfiles/agents/scheduler/pulse-ledger-lint.py --project <dir>
3. Reports CLEAN — the duplicate is never surfaced

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Lint flags >1 done per (PT day, row), scoped to done only
- [ ] PT bucketing via zoneinfo, with a regression test for the UTC-evening boundary
- [ ] done+quiet on one day does NOT trip it
- [ ] Runs across every pulse project, not just this one

title: tap linearb: the access token is EXPIRED, so pool 3's headroom is unmeasurable
description:
## Context
Found while building dotfiles-kecb, 2026-08-09. ~/.claude-work/.credentials.json carries an
`expiresAt` ~12h in the past; GET /api/oauth/usage with that token answers 401
`authentication_error`. The gateway arm cannot cover for it either — no request has been logged
under group 'work' or 'linearb' inside the reader's 6h freshness window, because the seat is idle.

So pool `linearb` reports state=unavailable today. That is the CORRECT behaviour (an unmeasurable
pool is never rolled into — a reader that scored the failed read as "0% used" would declare an
account it cannot authenticate to wide open), but it means the third rung of the ruled rollover
order primary > secondary > linearb is dark: if primary AND secondary both hit their ceilings, the
fleet stalls instead of reaching LinearB's subscription.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. `bash agents/lib/tap-headroom.sh --pool linearb` -> state=unavailable, reason
   "credential access token EXPIRED".
2. python3 -c on ~/.claude-work/.credentials.json shows expiresAt < now.

## The fix is a USE, not an edit
Claude Code refreshes its own OAuth token when it runs; nothing should rewrite that file from
outside (tap-headroom.sh deliberately does not attempt a refresh — rewriting a credential file
under a running client is a worse failure than an unmeasured pool). One `lb-claude` launch, or one
tick on the linearb seat, restores it.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] ~/.claude-work's token is live again and `tap-headroom.sh --pool linearb` reports a real
  state=ok with numbers
- [ ] Decide + record whether an idle tap's credential going stale should itself be surfaced (a
  pool that silently leaves the rollover order is the failure this bead is an instance of), or
  whether the loud `unavailable` verdict is sufficient
close_reason: Resolved by exactly the predicted mechanism: Zig launched the linearb seat (2026-08-10 ~01:1xZ), Claude Code refreshed its own OAuth token, no /login needed. Live evidence: tap-headroom.sh --pool linearb -> state=ok src=oauth u5h=0.0600 u7d=0.1400 fable=0.0400, TAP_HEADROOM_RESULT=ok. The rollover order's third rung (primary > secondary > linearb) is measurable again. Residual watch: an idle seat's token re-expires — the AC's staleness concern is inherent to the design (unmeasurable pool = never rolled into, which is correct); periodic use or a scheduled linearb tick keeps it lit.

title: Laurels — unfarmable recognition from durability and caught mistakes
description:
## Context

Recognition is absent. No player base, so praise must come from sources the
agent does not control. Ranked: (1) shipped-and-still-working — a bead closed
>=30 days ago whose artifact still passes its own check today; (2) a guard
that caught a real mistake; (3) Zig's spontaneous transcript praise,
harvested lagged, attributed to the seat; (4) cited-by-later-work, tiebreak.

Rejected as farmable: beads closed, commits, tests written, lines.

Unfarmability is mechanical: a seat may never write its own laurel file, the
harvest runs as a different seat, the file is append-only, and a laurel
carries no work, priority, or privilege — seeing one gives nothing to do.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] A weekly harvest emits laurels from sources (1) and (2) at minimum
- [ ] Laurels land in an append-only per-seat file, NOT a bead
- [ ] A seat's writes to its own laurel file are blocked, tested by attempting one
- [ ] Laurels are injected at SessionStart for that window
- [ ] No laurel carries priority, assignment, or a link to open work
- [ ] Emits `LAURELS_RESULT=<n harvested>/<n candidates>` on every terminal path
- [ ] Injection is byte-capped (at most N laurels, same discipline as $HARNESS_ONBOARD_BEAD_CAP / lib/context-emit.sh) — a laurel that costs context in every session forever is a tax, not a reward
- [ ] v1 sources are (1) durability via dotfiles-om9z and (2) caught mistakes via `Verdict: FIX-FIRST|REJECT` scrutiny lines (121 `## Scrutiny —` markers exist fleet-wide, machine-readable today); transcript praise (source 3) is DEFERRED — it needs Zig-in-the-loop judgment, i.e. load

title: decision: the shared settings.json model key is claude-opus-5[1m], canonicalized from an uncommitted drive-by
description:
## Context
`~/demesne/claude/settings.json` (surfaced as `~/.claude/settings.json`) is the
MACHINE-WIDE launch-time default: it decides what model, and critically what CONTEXT
WINDOW, every session started from now on gets. Per `dotfiles-cpqi`, the bare alias
`opus[1m]` is the 200,000-token window and the canonical `claude-opus-5[1m]` is the
1,000,000-token one. Nothing in the pane distinguishes them, the statusline names the
same model either way, so a 200k seat compacts repeatedly and never says why.

The fork found on 2026-08-14, mid-session, by the imc-aug26 seat:

- The COMMITTED value was `claude-fable-5[1m]`.
- The working tree held an UNCOMMITTED `opus[1m]`, persisted into the shared file by
  some session running `/model opus`. That is exactly the drive-by mechanism
  `dotfiles-cpqi` documents, arriving from a lane nobody can now identify.
- The tick settings (`~/.claude-tick/settings.json`) still hold `claude-fable-5[1m]`,
  which is why session-start reports a divergence on `model`.

So "fix the alias" had two defensible answers that mean different things: canonicalize
the accident to `claude-opus-5[1m]`, or restore the repo intent `claude-fable-5[1m]`.

## Decision
Set it to `claude-opus-5[1m]`, and do NOT run `sync-tick-settings.sh`.

## Why
Zig approved this specific value in-session, having been told the change as
"canonicalize the settings.json model key to claude-opus-5[1m] so future sessions get
the 1M window". The fable/opus fork was discovered only after that approval, while
reading the target before overwriting it. Restoring fable would have been a different
action than the one he approved, taken on information he did not have at the time, so
the fork is surfaced here rather than resolved silently in either direction.

`sync-tick-settings.sh` was withheld because it syncs the tick lane FROM this file:
running it would flip every pulse tick from fable to opus, a real and unrequested cost
change. The divergence session-start reports is now intentional rather than pending.

The actual harm the guard fires on, the silent 200k window, is fixed by either value,
so nothing about this decision leaves that defect open.

## Reversibility
One word, one commit. No migration, no state.

Seats are unaffected either way: `post-tool-model-guard.sh` resolves the seat pin in
`agents/seats.yml` through `seat-resolve.sh` FIRST and only falls back to this key for
windows the roster does not know. This key governs scratch windows, not seated ones.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Zig confirms opus (close this) or says fable (revert the one word, close this)
- [ ] If fable: re-check whether `sync-tick-settings.sh` should then run, since the
      divergence resolves on its own in that case
- [ ] Consider whether the drive-by is worth a guard of its own: a `/model` that
      persists a BARE alias into the shared key reintroduces the 200k defect silently,
      and `dotfiles-cpqi` documents the mechanism without preventing it
notes:
--- 2026-08-14, ANSWERED BY THE SENESCHAL. The value is FABLE, not opus. ---

This bead was filed naming a fork it could not resolve. The seneschal resolved it within the
hour: **Zig ratified `claude-fable-5[1m]` as the machine-wide default earlier the same evening**,
in a deliberate ruling, and it is recorded in the restoration runbook `dotfiles-w65x` step S2 to
be set once at the primary reset.

So the two approvals were not equal weight, and this bead's "Why" section over-read the one it
had. Zig's approval of opus came from picking which chores to run this session; the value sat
inside an option label he was not being asked to adjudicate. The seneschal's ruling is the
considered one. A considered ruling beats an incidental one, and I did not know the considered
one existed when I wrote the commit.

RESOLUTION, agreed with the seneschal rather than acted on unilaterally:
- The FORM half was right and stands. Canonicalizing `opus[1m]` -> a full `claude-*-5[1m]` id
  fixes the silent 200,000-token window, and that defect is orthogonal to which model is named.
- The VALUE is left for **S2 at the primary reset** to set to `claude-fable-5[1m]`. Deliberately
  NOT reverted here: two sessions thrashing a machine-wide launch-time key is worse than either
  value sitting there for a few hours, and S2 owns it.
- `sync-tick-settings.sh` still must not be run before S2. Once the shared key is fable it agrees
  with the tick settings on its own and the reported divergence disappears without a sync.

CONTEXT THAT ARRIVED WITH THE RULING and changes the picture:
The **work tap lost fable**. The LinearB marketing-team account was disabled (org moved to a
company-wide account) and `~/.claude-work` was re-authed 2026-08-14T00:57Z; `tap-headroom --pool
linearb` now reads `fable=-`, and `taps.work.failover` is `[]`, so a work-tap seat cannot borrow
it from personal either. A fable pin on a work-tap seat is currently UNSATISFIABLE and opus is the
ceiling there. That does not argue against fable as the shared default, because this key governs
windows the roster does not recognise rather than seated ones, but it does mean "fable everywhere"
is no longer true and the two facts are easy to conflate.

The third acceptance criterion below is the one still worth doing: nothing prevents the next
`/model <alias>` from persisting a BARE alias back into this key and silently reinstating the 200k
window. The form keeps being fixed by hand; that is the shape of defect that comes back.

title: daily-digest writes row:null on every ledger line — 30 invisible ticks
description:
Found 2026-07-26 while wiring the vault-sync alarm into harnessd's manifest.

`/home/ubuntu/explore/refs/digest-ledger.jsonl` has 30 lines and **every single one carries `"row": null`**. harnessd's manifest faithfully mirrors this: the `pulse-daily-digest` loop entry has `"ledger_row": null`.

This is a live instance of the exact defect the 2026-07-25 pass repaired — 23 null rows across 3 ledgers, traced to `pulse/SKILL.md` documenting `"row":null` in its own example (the "documented example IS the defect" class, dotfiles-mlti). That fix repaired the existing rows and the SKILL's example. **This ledger was missed**, and has kept writing nulls since.

WHY IT MATTERS: cap counters and every per-row analytic key on the row name. A null row is an invisible tick — it cannot be counted against a cap, cannot be attributed, and cannot be distinguished from a different loop's line in the same file. The only sanctioned escape hatch is the literal string `"unattributed"`, never null and never a guessed name.

Note this is NOT the same as the pulse ledger: /daily-digest writes its own `digest-ledger.jsonl`, which is likely why the earlier repair pass missed it — it was scoped to `pulse-ledger.jsonl`.

## Steps to Reproduce

    python3 -c "import json,collections;print(collections.Counter(json.loads(l).get('row') for l in open('/home/ubuntu/explore/refs/digest-ledger.jsonl') if l.strip()))"

Returns {None: 30}.

## Acceptance Criteria

- /daily-digest writes a real row name on every ledger line
- the 30 existing null rows are repaired (inferred with evidence, or the literal "unattributed" where genuinely unknowable)
- harnessd's manifest entry for pulse-daily-digest carries the real ledger_row instead of null
- pulse-ledger-lint.py (already promoted to dotfiles/agents/scheduler/) is pointed at digest-ledger.jsonl too, so this ledger is covered by the same guard
- a sweep for any OTHER ledger the original repair missed
notes:
## Fixed — 2026-07-26 (Opus-5 audit Wave 1)

Emitters fixed FIRST, then backfill — 4 sites: explore/.claude/skills/daily-digest/SKILL.md,
explore/bin/friction_ledger.py (new LEDGER_ROW constant), dotfiles recall-distill/SKILL.md,
and a new declarative 'Non-pulse ledger rows' table in explore/refs/pulse.md that makes the
row names CANONICAL (the lint discovers valid row names from any markdown table in that file;
verified pulse-cap.py / pulse-stall.py / ledger_streak.py do NOT parse those tables, so it
cannot make anything fire).

Backfill by textual insertion after ts — every other byte preserved (the three files use
different separator styles), with a per-line JSON round-trip assertion: digest-ledger 30
lines, friction-ledger 1, recall-distill-ledger 2. The last two were tracked by NO bead and
are the real answer to the bead's 'sweep for any OTHER ledger' criterion.

Verified: no ledger under refs/ has a null/empty/missing row; pulse-ledger-lint.py --selftest
passes; pulse-ledger.jsonl and digest-ledger.jsonl both lint CLEAN; pytest bin -q -> 106 passed.
close_reason: Fixed and merged in Wave 1. Two untracked ledgers found and fixed alongside.

title: bug: pulse-dispatch-remote leaks a tmux window per dispatch (lexicon glyph breaks the name match)
description:
## Context

The remote window lookup matched `#{window_name}` by splitting on whitespace and
comparing `$2`. The tmux-status hook PREFIXES the window name with a lexicon
glyph (🧠/✅/🔔/🌀), so `$2` is the GLYPH, never the row name. Every window that
had ever run a tick failed to match, and each dispatch silently created ANOTHER
window. Zig caught two live `weekly-report` windows on marketing-vps.

pulse-inject.sh had already solved this locally with `strip_lexicon()` and a
comment naming the trap; the remote script's comment claimed "same contract as
pulse-inject.sh" but the code never ported it.

Second defect found while fixing it: `\t` in a tmux `-F` format is NOT expanded
by tmux. pulse-inject.sh only works because bash `$'...'` expands it before
tmux sees it; that does not survive the ssh quoting round-trip, so a tab-
delimited fix emits a literal backslash-t and silently matches nothing.

Fixed: split on the first space (window_id never contains one), treat the
remainder as the name, strip a leading non-alphanumeric run. Generic strip
rather than a fixed glyph list so a new lexicon glyph cannot reintroduce it.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Dispatch any row to marketing-vps; the window is created with a plain name.
2. Let the tick run — the status hook decorates it to "✅ <row>".
3. Dispatch the same row again.
4. `ssh marketing-vps "tmux list-windows -t '=work'"` shows TWO windows for that row.
5. Repeat: one additional window per dispatch, unbounded.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [x] The matcher strips the lexicon glyph before comparing
- [x] No `\t` in the tmux -F format sent over ssh
- [x] Verified against live decorated windows: weekly-report -> @6, di-tuesday -> @5, dotfiles -> @0, vps-di -> @10
- [x] A genuinely absent row still returns empty so the window gets created
- [x] The leaked duplicate window on marketing-vps removed
close_reason: done

title: guard: refuse the raw-binary tap bypass (env ... CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=... claude)
description:
## Context
Measured 2026-08-09 19:23Z: `env -u CC_NO_GATEWAY CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=~/.claude-secondary claude -p ...`
run from inside a Claude Code session BILLED to secondary while the logged attribution said
personal. Two facts compose into it: `claude` is a shell FUNCTION and `env` runs the BINARY (a
function is not inherited by env), so the wrapper never executes; and Claude Code EXPORTS
ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS to its own children, so every Bash-tool shell inside a session starts
life carrying its parent's X-Tap.

dotfiles-kecb closed the two halves it could reach: the wrapper's declining launch branches now
`env -u ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS` instead of passing an inherited block through, and zsh/.zshenv
drops a wrapper-shaped inherited block in EVERY zsh (including the non-interactive Bash-tool
shell, which is where the poison lives). After that, a bypassed launch sends no header and logs as
`unknown` — visibly unattributed, which is recoverable, instead of confidently wrong, which is
not.

## What is still open
A raw-binary launch from a shell that never sourced either file — a foreign script, a cron entry,
another machine — still reaches the API with no attribution at all. That is the CORRECT failure
(an absent claim, not a false one), so this is not a P1. But the idiom is one an agent reaches for
naturally, it is already documented as wrong in ~/.zig-computer.zshenv's lb-claude note for a
different reason, and it produced the 19:23Z defect from an agent's own Bash tool.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. From inside a Claude Code session: `printenv ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS` -> the parent's block.
2. `env CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=~/.claude-secondary claude -p hi` -> billed to secondary, attributed to
   whatever the parent's X-Tap said (pre-kecb) or unattributed (post-kecb).
3. Correct idiom, for the block message to name: a SUBSHELL export plus the function —
   `( export CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=~/.claude-secondary; claude ... )`.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] A PreToolUse Bash guard refuses an invocation that sets CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR through `env` (or
  any prefix) around a `claude` that will resolve to the BINARY, and its block message carries the
  subshell idiom verbatim and copy-pasteable
- [ ] Fail-open on anything it cannot parse: this hook runs on every Bash call fleet-wide
- [ ] Hermetic suite + a mutant per repo rule 1; pre-commit arm

title: the PORTCULLIS + stacked-PR package — accept finished work centrally so builder seats hand off at commit-time (Zig idea package 2026-08-11)
description:
## Context
Zig idea package routed via seneschal mail (dotfiles.jsonl row 5, ref dotfiles-qnfk, 2026-08-11) — for beading and eventual design, NOT immediate build.

THE SHAPE: a PORTCULLIS (Yegge, https://yegge.ai/essays/the-shape-of-things-to-come/) — a system that ACCEPTS FINISHED WORK to close it out, so builder seats hand off at commit-time instead of idle-waiting on suites/merges/bead-closure. Yegge's crew worked 10-15 min then idled 45-60 min watching work land; the portcullis freed them. Its side effect (decoupling seats from their accomplishments) is what Laurels already fixes (dotfiles-qnfk) — so this would be the missing half of a loop Yegge validated end-to-end.

LIVE INSTANCES (2026-08-10/11): zf2q's close waited ~2h on a ledger-row watcher; the iyip merge held the seneschal through suites+mutants. With a portcullis both seats hand off and take new work.

PIECE TWO: STACKED PRs (https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/get-started/about-stacked-prs) in the subagent test/impl flow — split impl and test into small stacked PRs, queue MANY, then a Yegge 'landrush': merge a bunch at once and swarm bug fixes.

Zig's honest framing: solution-maybe-in-search-of-a-problem for solo repos, but (a) valuable where the repo is public or collaborative, (b) likely to yield agentic-coding-discipline insights, (c) we want the shape READY before a project needs it.

## Design constraints (from the mail, binding)
- The portcullis must RESPECT the guarded-merge sequence + the completion-notification cleanup gate (dotfiles-3135) — it CENTRALIZES that ritual, never bypasses it.
- Per-suite leak guards / commit gates become the portcullis's job, not the builder's.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Design study exists weighing portcullis vs current orchestrator-merges model, citing the live instances above
- [ ] Stacked-PR vibe card routed to ~/explore for the dive loop (Zig explicitly wants that angle explored)
- [ ] Sequenced behind current harness-repair work; surfaced to Zig before any build

## Write target
none (design study for Zig + a /dive lead already routed as explore-kri2). The eventual portcullis build would be ~/demesne scheduler tier — future beads after the design.

title: Restart-when-ready for pulse loops — a tick may request its own handoff
description:
## Context

Pulse loops already satisfy four of five handoff features: invocable by human
or agent, time to finish and write notes, and a harness restart primed with
the agent's own note (`pulse-inject.sh --fresh` sends `/clear`, then the tick
reads its note). Missing: the agent REQUESTING the restart — `--fresh` clears
unconditionally, so a tick mid-thought is cleared out from under itself.

Does not weaken the autonomous-loop exception: a handoff request is not an
escalation and never blocks on AskUserQuestion.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] A tick can end `outcome:"handoff-requested"` and drop `.handoff-ready--<window>`
- [ ] `--fresh` clears only when that marker is present, or a stated hard ceiling is hit
- [ ] No marker + no ceiling = pane left warm, reason logged to the ledger
- [ ] The ceiling is explicit and documented — a loop cannot refuse a handoff forever
- [ ] Made to fail on purpose: a tick requesting no handoff is verifiably NOT cleared
- [ ] The consent marker is window-scoped AND staleness-bounded: a marker older than the loop's own interval is ignored and logged as stale (a crashed tick must not authorize a /clear forever)

title: validate-seats: a fable pin on a work-tap seat is unsatisfiable but passes validation
description:
## Context

2026-08-14: the LinearB marketing-team account was disabled (org moved to a
company-wide LinearB account) and Zig re-authed ~/.claude-work into the new one.
The new account is NOT a premium seat — `tap-headroom --pool linearb` reports
`fable=-`, `subscriptionType: team`, `rateLimitTier: default_raven`.

Because `taps.work.failover` is `[]` — deliberately, so a LinearB schedule never
silently spends Zig's personal quota — a work-tap seat **cannot borrow fable from
personal either**. So `model: fable` on any work-tap seat is now
**unsatisfiable**, not merely expensive or unwise.

Today this is documented only as a COMMENT in the `taps.work:` block of
agents/seats.yml. That is the weakest rung of the derive/drop/assert/refuse
ladder, and this repo has already been bitten twice this week by superseded
comments in that very file: the roster header advertised a "linearb pins fable
for ALL seven schedules" amendment for a day after it stopped being true, and a
seat independently hypothesised that the model guard was matching comment text
because a stale model name sat above a live key.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Edit agents/seats.yml and set `model: fable` on any seat whose `tap: work`
   (linearb, imc-aug26, dev-interrupted).
2. Run `python3 agents/lib/validate-seats.py agents/seats.yml`.
3. Observe: **OK**. The validator gates `model:` against KNOWN_MODELS (the four
   aliases) and never cross-checks the pin against the tap's capability.
4. The failure only appears later, at launch, against an account that has no such
   model — and per the wrapper's fable leg reading ARGV, a mis-specified launch
   can silently fall back rather than erroring, so the seat may just quietly run
   something else.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] validate-seats REFUSES a `model:` pin the seat's tap cannot satisfy, with a
      message naming the seat, the pin, the tap, and why.
- [ ] The tap's model ceiling is DATA, not a hardcoded list — a `models:` or
      `max_model:` key on the tap block, so the next account change is a one-line
      edit rather than a code change.
- [ ] The check survives the tap gaining fable again (the ceiling rises) without
      code edits.
- [ ] Proven by a MUTANT THAT DIES on the case it names: a fable-on-work-tap
      roster must FAIL validation, and a legal roster must still PASS, in the
      same run. Model the harness on the existing seats mutation suite, which
      already covers FAILOVER and SEATTAP-CONSISTENCY — this is a sibling of
      those, not a new category.
- [ ] The `taps.work:` prose comment is trimmed to point at the mechanical check
      once it exists, rather than duplicating the rule.

## Notes

WHY IT IS ONLY P2 despite being a correctness gap: all three work-tap seats are
currently pinned `opus` and therefore legal, so nothing is broken right now. The
risk is entirely prospective — a future edit restoring a fable pin from memory or
from the stale amendment, which is precisely what nearly happened today.

RELATED, same family: `pool.linearb` in agents/scheduler/taps.conf should
probably carry the ceiling too, since that file is where pool facts live. Decide
whether the tap block or taps.conf is the single owner rather than putting it in
both — two copies of a capability fact is the defect this bead exists to prevent.

description:

The 200k window is the root multiplier on today's compaction thrash. The write path for the drift: Claude Code's /model command PERSISTS its choice to live settings — and post-tool-model-guard.sh's restore path instructs sessions to run /model with EXPECTED, which resolves from roster values that are ALIASES ("fable", "sonnet", "haiku" per pulse-models.jsonl). Zig's hypothesis ("the fable guards wrongly pick the model") confirmed as the loop, not the single writer.

## Steps to Reproduce

3. Every subsequently launched session runs the 200k base; statusline still says "Fable 5"; only guard math or a >200k context proves it.

- [ ] A single canonicalization table (alias -> full model id incl. [1m]) in one shared lib, consumed by: post-tool-model-guard.sh's restore instruction (instructs /model with the CANONICAL id, never an alias), pulse-inject's model launch path (--model passes canonical), and any seats.yml/roster resolution

title: a1111: upcast_attn insufficient for SDXL inpaint on MPS — escalate to --no-half
description:
## Context

Follow-up to dotfiles-43l (closed earlier today). 43l added
`upcast_attn: true` to config.json — the Settings-only toggle that the
NaN error message itself recommended. The fix was applied as documented
(file installed, LaunchAgent kickstarted, A1111 booted clean), but user
re-tested inpaint immediately after and the NaN still fires:

```
NansException: A tensor with NaNs was produced in Unet. ... Try setting
the "Upcast cross attention layer to float32" option in Settings >
Stable Diffusion or using the --no-half commandline argument to fix this.
```

Verified `~/stable-diffusion-webui/config.json` contains
`{"upcast_attn": true}` and the file is at the correct location. The
setting key matches A1111 source (`shared_options.py:182`). Despite all
that, the NaN check still trips on inpainting attempts. Likely cause:
on MPS, SDXL inpainting has additional fp16 underflow paths beyond the
cross-attention layer that the upcast doesn't cover.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. A1111 on pico per rp0 + 43l (config.json has `upcast_attn: true`)
2. Load SDXL base 1.0
3. Open Img2Img → Inpaint
4. Upload image, draw mask, generate (any prompt, default settings)
5. After ~14s, NansException fires

Repeatable: user has seen it on multiple consecutive inpaint attempts
since 43l's fix.

## Fix

Escalate from "upcast just the cross-attention layer" to "--no-half"
(full fp32 throughout the model). The error message lists this as the
alternative recommended remedy. Trade-off: SDXL memory footprint
doubles from ~6.5GB to ~13GB — fine on M1 Max with 64GB RAM.

Changes to `~/dotfiles/a1111/webui-user.sh`:
- Drop `--upcast-sampling` ("no effect with --no-half" per A1111's
  own help text)
- Add `--no-half`
- Keep `--no-half-vae` (was already there; redundant under --no-half
  but harmless)
- Keep `upcast_attn: true` in config.json as belt-and-suspenders;
  technically moot but doesn't hurt

## Regression guard

- Structural: webui-user.sh in dotfiles carries --no-half as part of
  COMMANDLINE_ARGS. Fresh-Mac rebuild (mac.setup.sh) installs the
  current webui-user.sh, so the fix is durable.
- Documentation: long-form comment in webui-user.sh explains WHY
  --no-half over --upcast-sampling (because the lighter path tested
  insufficient for SDXL inpaint on MPS in this real-world test).

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] webui-user.sh updated with --no-half
- [x] Pico's live webui-user.sh synced
- [x] LaunchAgent kickstarted, A1111 boots clean with new flag
- [ ] User re-tests inpaint, confirms NaN no longer fires
- [ ] Performance impact (memory + iteration speed) acceptable
notes:
## CLOSED 2026-05-24 — verified by user

User retested SDXL inpaint after --no-half landed; inpaint works, no
NaN. Performance impact deemed acceptable in the field (no complaint
on speed/memory; M1 Max 64GB carries the doubled SDXL footprint
without strain).

title: subagent watch-loops outlive completion and block worktree reaping — second occurrence
description:
## Context
Second confirmed occurrence (criterion set by the 2026-08-10 works-seat handoff: "one-off, bead if a second builder does it"). A completed worktree builder leaves a background poll-loop alive — `until tail -N <task-output> | grep -qE '...'; do sleep 15; done` — whose cwd pins the worktree, so pre-worktree-remove-guard (correctly) blocks reaping until an operator classifies the process from argv and kills it. Occurrence 1: 2026-08-09/10 prior works session, builder's self-deadlocked pgrep watch-loops (patterns matched each other's argv). Occurrence 2: 2026-08-10 this session, demesne builder (79zy) left a tail-grep loop watching its own background git-commit task file after final completion. The guard is WAI both times; the SUBAGENT HABIT is the defect — builders start unbounded monitors for their own background tasks and don't reap them before returning.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Dispatch a worktree subagent that backgrounds a long command and polls its output file with an `until ...; do sleep 15; done` loop
2. Let the agent complete and return its final summary without killing the loop
3. Attempt the standard cleanup: `git worktree remove --force --force <its worktree>` — pre-worktree-remove-guard blocks with the live pids

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Pick the layer: subagent definition/dispatch template gains a "reap your own background processes before final summary" contract, OR the guard learns to classify pattern-matched poll-loops (tail|grep|sleep argv, cwd in worktree, parent chain dead) as debris and allow with a note — decide with evidence, not both blindly
- [ ] Whichever layer: made to fail on purpose (a synthetic leftover loop is either prevented or auto-classified)
- [ ] The operator playbook (classify from argv → kill → reap) recorded where the guard's block message points

title: decision: upgrade default opus alias 4.8[1m] → opus-5[1m] (all pulse loops + interactive)
description:
Context: Zig asked "upgrade all system pulses to opus 5" (2026-07-25). The explore vibe-explore tick #117 (and every pulse loop) had been running claude-opus-4-8[1m]. Investigation: pulse sessions launch bare `claude` (pulse-inject LAUNCH="claude"; the claude identity-wrapper function adds no --model), so they inherit CC's default opus alias. That alias is pinned by ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL, set from CC_GW_MODEL in ~/dotfiles/bash/.bash_aliases and injected into ~/.claude/settings.json .env by cc-gw (see dotfiles-w1r for why the pin exists: it survives resume behind the pico gateway, which disables CC's auto-1M-upgrade; [1m] is a beta header, not a distinct model).

Decision: changed CC_GW_MODEL "claude-opus-4-8[1m]" → "claude-opus-5[1m]" AND updated the live ~/.claude/settings.json .env.ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL to match. Preserved the [1m] (1M-context) suffix rather than dropping to plain opus-5 (200K), to keep the current context posture. Verified claude-opus-5[1m] resolves + is served through the gateway (headless -p PONG, exit 0).

Why: it's the single lever for the opus-alias default that ALL bare-`claude` launches inherit — there is no per-pulse model config to flip; pulses and interactive sessions share this default. Preserving [1m] avoids a silent context downgrade. Only changes the `opus` ALIAS, so explicit /model and --model picks still win (same property dotfiles-w1r relied on).

Scope note: this upgrades the opus default for EVERYTHING that doesn't explicitly pick a model — pulses AND Zig's interactive sessions — because that's the only lever. Judged in-scope with intent (opus-5 is strictly the better default). 

Reversibility: trivial. `cc-direct` scrubs the pin; or edit CC_GW_MODEL / settings.json .env back to 4-8[1m] (backup at ~/.claude/settings.json.bak-opus5-*). One-line revert.

Effect timing: env is read at CC launch, so this takes effect on the NEXT launch of each session. Currently-live durable pulse windows (explore, elevate, daily-digest) keep 4.8[1m] until restarted or switched via /model claude-opus-5[1m]. Left the live-window switch as a follow-up for Zig (restarting warm sessions, incl. his interactive one, is his call).

title: mail: per-sender daily cap and unread-dedupe, as refusals
description:
## Context
Every durable mail is a git commit in the JSONL. The reference measured *"4
agents x 15 patrol cycles x 2 mails per cycle = 120 commits just for routine
chatter"* and answered it with a per-role budget TABLE agents are asked to
honor. Ours should be mechanical instead: the script refuses.

Two rules: a per-sender daily cap on DURABLE mail (nudge and ephemeral
uncapped), and a refusal of a second mail with the same `(from, to, subject)`
while the first is unread — which kills the reference's "duplicate escalations"
anti-pattern without asking anyone to check their outbox.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Over-cap send prints `MAIL_SEND_RESULT=refused-budget` and creates nothing
- [ ] Duplicate unread send prints `MAIL_SEND_RESULT=refused-duplicate`
- [ ] Refusals are exit-0 verdicts, not errors
- [ ] Both refusals demonstrated by deliberately triggering them
- [ ] Models the cap on ~/explore/bin/pulse-cap.py's THREE-valued discipline (0 under-cap fire / 1 at-cap quiet / 2 ledger-unreadable BLOCKED — never silently treated as under-cap); a binary check is the named anti-pattern

title: mail: defer groups / queues / channels; ship directed mail only
description:
## Context
Gas Town ships three bead-backed fan-out primitives — groups (`hq-group-*`),
queues (`hq-q-*`), channels (`hq-channel-*`) — with an address resolution order
that errors rather than guesses on an ambiguous bare name.

**Decision: ship directed mail only; do not build groups, queues, or channels
on day one.**

Why. Queues already exist here: `br ready` + `br update --claim` is atomic
assign with exactly-one-claimant semantics, and a `queue:` primitive would be a
second, worse tracker inside the tracker. Channels need subscriber lists,
retention counts, and a pruning patrol — three moving parts for zero current use
case. Groups are the only near-term-plausible one and are cheap when needed (a
group is a label; `br list --label-any` already ships), so waiting costs little.
Decisively: the reference's own 120-commits-a-day cost figure is a FAN-OUT
number — shipping fan-out first imports the problem ahead of the need.

Adopted regardless of tier: **ambiguous names error rather than guess.**

Alternatives considered. (a) Ship groups with directed mail — cheap, but adds a
membership registry to maintain with one human and a handful of sessions.
(b) Ship all three for parity with the reference — parity is not a requirement;
Gas Town runs many long-lived role agents, we do not.

Reversibility: high. Labels are additive; a group can be introduced later
without changing a single delivered message.
notes:
## REVERSED — 2026-08-09, Zig, in-session (2cc9586e): "un-defer fan-out groups/queues/channels" (his completed reason 2026-08-09: 'bc i think we'd benefit from them'; the standing context: charters/seats/seneschal/marshal landed since this deferral, and each creates a natural fan-out consumer — a charter IS a group (@household, @inquiry), the seneschal broadcasts the brief, the marshal fans work to a fleet).
Consequences:
- Fan-out moves from DEFERRED to IN-SCOPE V2 of the mail epic: directed mail still ships FIRST (c6mp/3kt6/axfb/jbpp unchanged — v1), fan-out specs against the charter registry once it exists (group = charter or office, never a hand-maintained list — the two-copies rule applied to membership).
- The spec addition rides c6mp or a sibling: group addressing grammar (@<charter>, @all), delivery semantics (fan-out at SEND time into per-seat inboxes — no shared-inbox races), and the budget bead f0ih's caps apply per-recipient.
- Reversibility: high — nothing built either way yet; this re-opens scope, not code.

title: mail: mail-send.sh — nudge-first with automatic fallback to a bead
description:
## Context
The send path. Resolves the address (identity track's resolver), attempts
`pulse-inject.sh`, parses the LAST `PULSE_INJECT_RESULT=` line from stdout, and
falls back to a `type=message` bead in `~/mail` on anything other than

one layer down.

Reuses the existing ephemeral channel; does not reinvent it.

      (`nudged` / `mailed:<id>` / `refused-budget` / `refused-duplicate` /
      `failed-*`)

title: mail: the transport contract — three tiers, verdicts, and the envelope
description:
## Context
Formal spec for the transport, written against an OPAQUE address (the identity
track owns the grammar; this spec must not invent one). Covers: the three
delivery tiers (nudge / ephemeral bead / durable bead); the fallback ladder
driven by `PULSE_INJECT_RESULT`; the fail-closed rule that exit-0-without-a-marker
means NOT delivered; the message schema (subject prefix + key-value body +
freeform, per Gas Town's format conventions); ack-by-close; and the envelope
that marks a nudge as agent-originated.

Adapted litmus test, verbatim in spirit: *if the recipient's session dies and
restarts, do they need this message?* Yes → mail. No → nudge.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Spec bead states all three tiers with their commit cost and their
      durability scope (ephemeral = this box only)
- [ ] Fallback ladder enumerates every `PULSE_INJECT_RESULT` value and its routing
- [ ] Message schema documented with >=2 worked examples
- [ ] Names exactly what it needs from the identity track (grammar, resolver,
      whoami, multi-session tiebreak) as explicit inputs
- [ ] The spec enumerates the canonical MAIL_SEND_RESULT= verdict vocabulary (nudged / mailed:<id> / refused-budget / refused-duplicate / failed-*) — moved OUT of axfb's AC, which then references this spec
- [ ] The three-vs-two tier mismatch is RESOLVED in the spec: either define what distinguishes an 'ephemeral bead' from a durable one (retention? no-commit?) or collapse to two tiers (nudge / bead) — axfb currently implements two while this spec names three
- [ ] The envelope section absorbs dotfiles-nudge-envelope-3427's requirement verbatim (agent-originated inject distinguishable from a Zig turn, verified by a decline test) — 3427 then tracks only the pulse-inject implementation once the format is fixed here
- [ ] States when a mail bead legitimately DOES commit (the zero-commit-chatter criterion is currently true only because nudge-success is assumed; make the boundary explicit)
- [ ] Names dotfiles-seat-address-spec-uikg as the address-grammar input: the mail `to:` IS the seat address — one grammar, no parallel invention. uikg must answer: foreign-seat lookup (resolve OTHERS, not self), unresolvable recipient (a failed-* verdict, not a guess), and whether a seat with no live window is still addressable (durable mail says yes)
